entries.topic: Spanish, Portuguese and Roman Inquisitions: founding, targets, figures, abolition

claims.text: Sixtus IV's bull Exigit sincerae devotionis affectus (1 November 1478) let Ferdinand and Isabella name inquisitors; first inquisitors Miguel de Morillo and Juan de San Martín named 27 September 1480; first auto de fe at Seville 6 February 1481, six burned alive; Torquemada named Inquisitor General 17 October 1483; Council of the Suprema created 1483, members named by the crown; inquisitor general designated by the crown.

Sixtus IV's bull of 18 April 1482 criticised abuses in Aragon (Lea: 'the most extraordinary bull in the history of the Inquisition'); Ferdinand replied 13 May 1482 doubting its authenticity; the pope suspended it.
Alhambra Decree 31 March 1492 by Isabella and Ferdinand: Jews to convert or leave by 31 July 1492; 40,000-100,000 expelled (estimates); symbolically revoked 16 December 1968.

Moriscos: Granada conversion decree 1502; Alpujarras revolt 1568-71; expulsion ordered by Philip III 1609, about 300,000 expelled; Protestant groups at Valladolid and Seville 1558-62, about 120 people, about 100 executions; alumbrados trials led to prison, no executions; Spanish indexes 1551, 1559, 1583 and later.

Contreras and Henningsen (1986), from the relaciones de causas: 44,674 trials 1540-1700, 826 executed in person, 778 in effigy; Kamen: no more than 3,000 executions overall, c.2,000 in the first forty years; Pérez: 125,000 trials, fewer than 10,000 executions; Monter (1990): 2,750 executions; Llorente (1817): 31,912 burned; García Cárcel: 4,200-5,250; Ereticopedia's own synthesis c.7,300 executions in person 1480-1820, c.4,500 confirmed.

Abolition: Napoleon's Chamartín decrees 4 December 1808; Cortes of Cádiz 22 February 1813; restored by Ferdinand VII 1814; abolished 9 March 1820; not revived after 1823, bishops' Juntas de Fe instead; final abolition decree 15 July 1834 (Martínez de la Rosa government, signed by Regent María Cristina).
Cayetano Ripoll, Catalan schoolmaster, deist, condemned by the Junta de Fe of Valencia and hanged 26 July 1826, the last person executed in Spain for heresy.
Manuel I of Portugal decreed 5 December 1496 that Jews convert or leave; in 1497 Jews were prevented from leaving and forcibly baptised; Lisbon massacre 1506 of about 2,000.

Portuguese Inquisition established 23 May 1536 by Paul III's bull Cum ad nihil magis at the request of John III; grand inquisitor chosen by the king; first auto da fé 1540; tribunals Lisbon, Évora, Coimbra, Goa; mainly New Christians; Almeida (1923): 31,457 sentences 1536-1794, 1,183 executed in person, 663 in effigy; Lea: 1,175 burned alive; Pombal ended limpeza de sangue 1773-74; abolished 31 March 1821 by the Constituent Cortes.

Cisneros had the contents of the Granada madrasa library burned in a public bonfire in the Bib-Rambla square in 1499; several Nasrid royal manuscripts thought burned survive, the royal library having been taken into exile by Boabdil (Ženka).

Roman Inquisition: Paul III's bull Licet ab initio, 21 July 1542, six cardinals incl. Gian Pietro Carafa; Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office under Sapienti consilio 29 June 1908; Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith by Integrae servandae 7 December 1965, shifting from punishing error to promoting faith; initially a tribunal 'exclusively for cases of heresy and schism'.
Andrea Del Col estimates about 1,250 death sentences among 51,000-75,000 cases judged in Italy after 1542; renamed Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith 2022.

At the Vatican presentation of the symposium volume (June 2004) Agostino Borromeo said Spain held about 125,000 trials and about 1% of defendants were executed; in Portugal of more than 13,000 tried in the 16th and early 17th c., 5.7% condemned to death.

Audit: Spanish Inquisition article says most of those labelled 'Lutheran' were not actual Protestants; irreligious acts, drunken mockery or anticlerical comments were marked 'Lutheran'; Protestant communities at Valladolid and Seville 1558-62 about 120 people; several autos de fe with about 100 executions.

entries.topic: Goa Inquisition 1560-1812, temple destruction, Konkani, Diamper

claims.text: Francis Xavier wrote to John III (dated 1545 by some, 1546 by others) asking that the king 'institute the holy Inquisition' (Neill); historians disagree whether he sought a tribunal or a minister for Christianity; he died 1552; canonised 12 March 1622.

Goa Inquisition established 1560 (first inquisitor Aleixo Dias Falcão, sent by Cardinal Henrique); original target New Christians; later Hindu converts accused of crypto-Hinduism became the main focus (Saraiva c.74%; Lehner over three-quarters involving public Hindu worship).

Temple destruction: order 30 June 1541 to destroy temples and give property to missionaries; royal order 8 March 1546 banning Hindu worship and feasts; by 1566 about 160 temples razed on Goa island; c.300 in Bardez by Franciscans 1566-67; c.300 in Salcete (evidence conflicts); 1569 royal letter said all temples burnt and razed; exact figures unavailable.

Laws of 1567 restricted Hindus incl. ban on Hindu priests officiating weddings; Konkani ban decreed by the viceroy 27 June 1684 at Franciscan urging, confirmed by the king 17 March 1687; renewed 1745 and 1812.

Last auto de fé 7 February 1773; suspended 1774, restored 1778; abolished 1812; records mostly burned after abolition; c.16,000 tried 1561-1774 (unsourced); 3,800 cases 1561-1623 (Benton); 57 burned in person and 64 in effigy (Machado; Saraiva; Parker & Starr-LeBeau); 71 autos de fé.
The Mangueshi linga was moved secretly from Kushasthali (Cortalim) to Priol, under Adil Shah's rule, in 1560 to escape temple destruction.
Goa CM Pramod Sawant said on 21 December 2021 that temples destroyed by the Portuguese need to be rebuilt.

Célia Tavares: Baião and Priolkar overstated the Inquisition's power; Dellon's account shaped the black legend; Goa handled many more cases than the metropolitan tribunals with similar conviction rates; no Jesuit served as inquisitor in Goa; Brahmins punished more harshly than lower-caste converts.
Priolkar, The Goa Inquisition (1961): Boxer called it dispassionate and objective; Délio de Mendonça and Dale Luis Menezes criticised it (methodologically flawed, reliance on Buchanan).

Synod of Diamper 20-27 June 1599 under Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes of Goa; 153 priests, 660 lay representatives, over 200 decrees aligning the Saint Thomas Christians with Rome; books judged heretical consigned to the flames during his tour; extent of loss hard to determine (Takahashi). Decree XIV forbade keeping, translating or reading Syriac books by 'Nestorian heretics'; banned books included an Infancy gospel and the Nomocanon of Abdisho; three Nomocanon manuscripts survive (Walters).

Audit: an appeal to start the Inquisition in Portuguese India was sent by Vicar General Miguel Vaz; the 1684 Konkani decree required people to speak Portuguese within three years, penalty imprisonment; when the Inquisition ended in 1812 the majority of its records were destroyed by Portuguese officials; the lead names Old Christians accused of Protestant involvement among those targeted; sodomy suspects given the second most harsh punishments; the article dates Xavier's letter 20 January 1545 from Malacca in one place and 1546 in another.

Audit: Tavares: in Goa it was very common to persecute local people not converted to Catholicism, 'quite disconcerting at first sight for the historian'; capital punishment (relaxation to the secular arm, burning) was the ultimate penalty for Christians of the Land; more often whippings, obligatory Sunday Mass and other corporal punishments, or galley sentences of 4-5 years that often ended in death, all with public humiliation at autos da fe; Brahmins treated more harshly than lower castes.

entries.topic: Inquisition and extirpation of idolatries in the Americas

claims.text: Maní: in May 1562 idols and bones found in a cave; by July investigators questioned 6,300 Maya, many under torture; more than 4,500 punished; at least 157 died, 32 maimed, dozens by suicide; auto de fe Sunday 12 July 1562 burned 27 codices, 64 effigies and 114 sets of exhumed bones; Toral ended the campaign October 1562; 2015 excavation found smashed incense burners, mostly from Mayapán; Landa head of Franciscans 1561, bishop 1572; more than 100 codices destroyed in the colonial period, at most four survive.
Landa wrote that the books contained 'nothing in which there were not to be seen superstition and lies of the devil' and 'we burned them all, which they regretted to an amazing degree'.

Landa was sent back to Spain to answer for an illegal inquisition; the Council of the Indies condemned his actions; a committee absolved him in 1569; Relación written c.1566, surviving copy c.1660; his 'alphabet' later helped Knorozov's syllabic decipherment in the 1950s.
Four Maya codices survive: Dresden, Madrid, Paris and the Grolier; the Grolier (Maya Codex of Mexico) declared authentic by INAH in 2018 and dated 1021-1154 CE, a Venus almanac.

Don Carlos Ometochtzin, Texcoco noble, burned 30 November 1539 on Zumárraga's order; Zumárraga reprimanded; trial led to Indigenous people being removed from inquisitorial jurisdiction; recent scholarship reads the case as a family and political dispute.

Philip II excluded Indians from the Inquisition in 1571; extirpation campaigns in Peru 1609-21, 1625-26, 1646-70; Ávila and the Huarochirí Manuscript; Villagómez; Mills: 'perhaps the most sustained religious persecution' of Indigenous people; Griffiths; mummies and objects burned; Andean religion survived by adaptation.

Mexico City tribunal established 4 November 1571 (Pedro Moya de Contreras); no jurisdiction over Indians except printed material in Indigenous languages; c.50 executions (González Obregón 51); Carvajal family burned 8 December 1596; auto of 11 April 1649; abolished 1820.

Lima tribunal established 9 January 1570, Indigenous people outside its jurisdiction; abolished 1813, restored 1815, ended 1820; Lima tribunal 1570-1820 focused on crypto-Judaism; 1639 Auto General de Fe (Schaposchnik).

Cartagena tribunal set up 1610 for New Granada and the Caribbean; 56 tried for witchcraft in its first 50 years, 52 of African descent; Paula de Eguiluz sentenced 30 November 1624 to 200 lashes, later perpetual imprisonment.

Third Council of Lima (1582-83, Toribio de Mogrovejo) ordered quipus containing non-Christian ceremonial matter destroyed ('pernicious instruments') while encouraging quipus for confession and doctrine; trilingual catechism in Spanish, Quechua, Aymara.

Sahagún gathered material from elders 1559-65; Florentine Codex finished 1575-77, 12 books in Nahuatl and Spanish, 2,446 pages, 2,472 illustrations, named Nahua collaborators; Philip II ordered such manuscripts confiscated in 1577; now in the Laurentian Library, Florence.
Itzcoatl (r.1427-1440) ordered historical codices burned, 'not wise that all the people should know the paintings' (Sahagún's informants, via León-Portilla).

García Icazbalceta (1881) defended Zumárraga against the charge of burning Aztec codices: most destruction before his arrival, no chronicler mentions his burnings, and the burning described by Alva Ixtlilxochitl was done by Tlaxcalans in 1520.

Pablo José de Arriaga SJ (1564-1622) published La extirpación de la idolatría del Pirú in Lima in 1621 (Gerónimo de Contreras), a manual for eradicating Andean religion that records its deities and rites as an eyewitness.

Audit: Becker: Griffiths views the campaigns, given their irregular appearance, as 'aberrations, not a commonplace phenomenon'; victims were whipped, exiled or even executed; mummies and artefacts burned; Villagómez's period the zenith; the Huarochirí Manuscript, in Quechua, drafted under Ávila to prosecute the practices it records.

Audit: Carlos Ometochtzin was a grandson of Nezahualcoyotl through Nezahualpilli; pleaded guilty to sexual charges, denied idolatry to the end; recent scholarship reads the trial as a family feud and local politics.
Audit: nine members of the extended Carvajal family were burned on the Zócalo on 8 December 1596.

Audit: Paula de Eguiluz was born enslaved in Santo Domingo; sentenced 30 November 1624 to 200 lashes, two years' penance working in Cartagena's hospital and exile from Cuba; final sentence perpetual imprisonment.
Audit: burning the codices allowed the Mexica state to develop a state-sanctioned history venerating Huitzilopochtli (Wikipedia, citing León-Portilla; Tlacaelel's role as instigator is unproven).

Audit: the Third Council of Lima text (via Lisi 1990, p.191) says the quipos contain testimonies of ancient superstition in which they keep the secrets of their rites, ceremonies and laws, and that the bishops must destroy them completely as pernicious instruments.
